lead: A three-phase supply is three sinusoids of equal RMS value and frequency, spaced 120° apart. At every instant their powers add to a constant, and in a balanced load their currents cancel in the neutral. That lets a balanced system be solved as one phase. An unbalanced load breaks the cancellation: the neutral point shifts, currents differ, and you must solve each phase and add phasors. The idea runs office wiring, 400 V motors, data-centre UPS systems and the grid itself.
prereq: You need: phasors for 120° shifts, impedance for per-phase Z, and single-phase power for cos φ.

sections.h3: Phase sequence, star and delta quantities

blocks.text: A three-phase source has three voltages of the same RMS value and frequency. Their phase angles are 0°, −120° and +120°. The order in which they reach their peaks is the phase sequence: a-b-c means phase a peaks first, then b 120° later, then c. Reverse two lines and the sequence becomes a-c-b; motors then run backwards.
V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub> (star); V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub> (delta)
blocks.where: V<sub>ph</sub> is the RMS phase voltage across one branch; V<sub>L</sub> is the RMS line-to-line voltage; I<sub>ph</sub> is the RMS current inside one phase branch; I<sub>L</sub> is the RMS current in one line conductor.

blocks.text: In a star (wye) connection each phase branch sits between one line and the neutral. The phase voltage V<sub>ph</sub> is line-to-neutral; the line voltage V<sub>L</sub> is between two lines. In a delta connection each branch sits between two lines, so the phase voltage equals the line voltage. There is no neutral in a three-wire delta.

For balanced positive sequence, the star line voltage V<sub>ab</sub> leads V<sub>an</sub> by 30°. In delta, the line current I<sub>a</sub> lags the phase current I<sub>ab</sub> by 30°. Keep the √3 with the line quantity that is larger: voltage in star, current in delta.

A balanced load has equal impedance in every phase: same |Z| and same angle φ. The three phase currents are equal in RMS and 120° apart. Their phasor sum is zero, so the neutral current is zero in a four-wire star system.

items: Identify the connection and write the per-phase impedance Z = R + jX.
Choose phase a. Find V<sub>ph</sub>: V<sub>L</sub>/√3 for star, V<sub>L</sub> for delta.
Find I<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>/Z and the angle φ = angle of Z. In star I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>; in delta I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>.
Find total real power P = 3 V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ and reactive power Q = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> sin φ.

blocks.text: The per-phase equivalent is a single-phase circuit with the phase voltage and one Z. Total power is three times the per-phase power. The formula √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ works for both star and delta because the √3 and the current or voltage ratio cancel. If a delta load must be replaced by an equivalent star, use the star-delta transformation from Unit 1, Foundations.

An unbalanced load has different Z in the three phases, or different phase angles. The currents no longer add to zero. In a four-wire star system with a solid neutral, each phase voltage is fixed by the supply, so each phase current is found on its own: I<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>a</sub>/Z<sub>a</sub>, I<sub>b</sub> = V<sub>b</sub>/Z<sub>b</sub>, I<sub>c</sub> = V<sub>c</sub>/Z<sub>c</sub>. The neutral current is the phasor sum I<sub>N</sub> = I<sub>a</sub> + I<sub>b</sub> + I<sub>c</sub>. It is generally not zero.

blocks.where: V<sub>N′N</sub> is the shift of the load star point N′ from the source neutral N; V<sub>a</sub>, V<sub>b</sub>, V<sub>c</sub> are source phase voltages; Y<sub>a</sub> = 1/Z<sub>a</sub>, Y<sub>b</sub> = 1/Z<sub>b</sub>, Y<sub>c</sub> = 1/Z<sub>c</sub> are phase admittances.

blocks.text: When the neutral is absent or has impedance, the star point N′ of the load shifts. Use Millman's theorem to find V<sub>N′N</sub>, then the load phase voltage is V<sub>a</sub> − V<sub>N′N</sub>. Compute each current and add them phasor-wise.

A three-wire delta has no neutral. Solve it by mesh currents around the three loops, or convert the delta load to an equivalent star and use the neutral-shift method. For any general unbalanced network, symmetrical components split the system into positive, negative and zero sequences; that method belongs to a power-systems course. This chapter stops at per-phase and mesh solutions.

figure.caption: The test for balance decides the method: a balanced load reduces to one per-phase circuit, while an unbalanced load needs a neutral-shift or mesh solution and phasor addition for the neutral current. The source values match the worked example.

spec.aria: A decision flow: a three-phase source is tested for balance; a balanced load goes to one per-phase circuit and then total power, an unbalanced load goes to a neutral-shift solution with unequal phase currents.

nodes.label: Load balanced?
nodes.note: equal Z per phase; currents 120° apart

examples.question: A balanced star-connected load of Z = 10 + j6 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply. Find the phase current, line current, total real power and neutral current.
steps: Line voltage V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V. For star, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 = 400/1.732 = 230.9 V.
In star, line current I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub> = 19.8 A.
Per-phase real power P<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ = 230.9 × 19.8 × 0.857 ≈ 3.92 kW.
Total real power P = 3 × 3.92 = 11.76 kW. Check: √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ = 1.732 × 400 × 19.8 × 0.857 = 11.76 kW.
The three currents are equal and 120° apart. Their phasor sum is zero, so neutral current I<sub>N</sub> = 0 A.
examples.answer: I<sub>ph</sub> = I<sub>L</sub> = 19.8 A, total real power P = 11.76 kW, neutral current I<sub>N</sub> = 0 A.
examples.check:
import math
VL = 400.0
Z = complex(10, 6)
Vph = VL / math.sqrt(3)
Zmag = abs(Z)
Iph = Vph / Zmag
phi = math.degrees(math.atan2(Z.imag, Z.real))
cosphi = math.cos(math.radians(phi))
P = 3 * Vph * Iph * cosphi
print(round(Iph, 1))
print(round(P / 1000, 2))
print(0.0)

traps: Using V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub> for a delta load, or I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub> for a star load. The √3 belongs to line voltage in star and line current in delta.
Assuming the neutral current is zero after the load becomes unbalanced. It is zero only when the three phase currents are equal and 120° apart.
Forgetting the 30° shift between line and phase quantities in the phasor diagram: star line voltage leads phase voltage; delta line current lags phase current for a-b-c sequence.
Computing total power as one phase power. A balanced three-phase load has P = 3 × per-phase P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ.
Applying the per-phase equivalent to an unbalanced star without a neutral. The neutral point shifts; find V<sub>N′N</sub> first.

quiz.a: The order in which the three phase voltages reach their positive peaks, such as a-b-c: a first, then b 120° later, then c.

quiz.q: Why is the neutral current zero in a balanced four-wire star system?
quiz.a: The three phase currents have equal RMS values and are 120° apart. Three equal phasors 120° apart add to zero, so their sum in the neutral is zero.

quiz.q: A balanced star load of Z = 8 + j6 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V line supply. Find the phase current and total real power.
The neutral wire of a four-wire star system opens while the load is unbalanced. What happens to the load phase voltages and the neutral current?
quiz.a: The load star point is no longer held at the source neutral. The neutral current in the opened wire is zero. Because no current can return, the three load currents must now sum to zero at the load star point; the star point shifts to a new voltage V<sub>N′N</sub>, which makes the three load phase voltages unequal and unequal currents whose phasor sum is zero.

quiz.q: A balanced delta load of Z = 30∠30° Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V line supply. Find the phase current and line current.
quiz.a: In delta V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V. I<sub>ph</sub> = 400/30 = 13.33 A. I<sub>L</sub> = √3 × 13.33 = 23.09 A.

quiz.q: Why does P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ work for both star and delta balanced loads?
quiz.a: In star V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>; in delta V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>. Substituting either pair into √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ gives 3 V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ.

quiz.q: Write the line-to-phase relations for star voltage and delta current.
quiz.a: Star: V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>. Delta: I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, unbalanced three-phase loads are studied with symmetrical components and load-flow programs, because neutral shift and negative-sequence current heat motors and trip relays. Power-quality engineers search for neutral current in office buildings fed by many small single-phase loads. Next topics to search: symmetrical components, neutral point displacement, unbalanced load flow, and negative-sequence relay settings.
